strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: reducing excessive chain-of-thought generation in large reasoning models while preserving or improving accuracy.
The proposed DEER method is simple, training-free, and practically appealing: monitor reasoning transition tokens, induce a trial answer, and stop when confidence is high.

Empirical results on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models show substantial reductions in generated reasoning length, often 30-43%, with reported accuracy improvements across math, science, and coding benchmarks.

The paper includes useful analyses of early-exit behavior, threshold sensitivity, different transition signals, programming tasks, and a non-DeepSeek model, which helps clarify when the method works and where it is brittle.
The qualitative examples make the overthinking failure mode intuitive and show why early termination can sometimes improve correctness rather than only efficiency.
weaknesses: The evaluation lacks several necessary baselines for a top-tier venue. Comparisons are mostly against vanilla CoT, with no strong empirical comparison to budget forcing, concise prompting, adaptive compute methods, early stopping/self-consistency variants, or the closely related concurrent early-exit methods discussed in related work.

The reported generation-length metric appears to count final output length but may not fully account for the extra trial-answer generations and confidence evaluations. This risks overstating efficiency gains unless total generated/evaluated tokens and wall-clock costs are reported comprehensively.

The branch-parallel decoding acceleration is described as part of the method but is not actually evaluated; the paper says more latency analysis will be added in a forthcoming version. This leaves a key efficiency claim under-supported.

The confidence definition is underspecified and somewhat questionable: Equation 3 uses the maximum token probability over the vocabulary rather than the probability of the generated answer token, which may not faithfully measure confidence in the trial answer. The paper needs clearer justification and ablations of alternative confidence scores.

Hyperparameter and implementation details are incomplete. The choice of threshold, transition-token set, answer-inducer prompt, stopping criteria, and whether thresholds are tuned per model/task are not sufficiently specified for strong reproducibility.

Several benchmark results rely on small test sets such as AIME 2024 and AMC 2023, where gains of a few questions can look large. The paper does not provide confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated runs despite using greedy decoding on high-variance tasks.
The method is less robust outside the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family: QwQ-32B shows reduced length but worse accuracy, suggesting model-specific dependence on formatting and end-of-thinking behavior.

The novelty is moderate. The core idea is a useful decoding-time heuristic, but it is close in spirit to budget forcing and contemporaneous trial-answer/probe-based early-exit methods; stronger positioning and direct comparisons are needed.

There are presentation and maturity issues, including references to missing or forthcoming content, placeholder-like mentions such as Table X, and some unclear algorithmic descriptions around rollback/reversion after trial-answer induction.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: reducing excessive test-time reasoning in long-CoT reasoning models while preserving or improving answer accuracy.
The proposed DEER mechanism is simple, training-free, and potentially easy to integrate with models whose reasoning format exposes transition tokens such as "Wait" and end-of-thinking delimiters.
The manuscript includes experiments across several DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen model sizes and multiple benchmark types, including math, science QA, and programming tasks.

The paper provides some useful diagnostic analyses, including threshold sensitivity, alternative transition tokens, fine-grained correct/incorrect outcome categories, and qualitative examples illustrating overthinking failures.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not convincing enough for a top-tier venue. The main comparison is largely against vanilla zero-shot CoT, while obvious baselines such as fixed budget forcing, static early exit at matched token budgets, concise prompting, s1-style budget controls, adaptive compute methods, and other CoT compression or early-stopping approaches are missing or underdeveloped.

The efficiency claims are potentially misleading because it is unclear whether generation length and cost include all induced trial-answer tokens and repeated confidence-evaluation computation. Since DEER may generate trial answers at many transition points, final-output length alone is not an adequate compute metric.

The proposed branch-parallel decoding acceleration is described but apparently not implemented or evaluated; the paper explicitly says more latency analysis with vLLM and the acceleration strategy will be added in a future version. This leaves a central practical claim incomplete.

The method appears brittle and model-format dependent. It relies on specific transition tokens and end-of-thinking delimiters; results degrade on QwQ-32B, where DEER reduces length but makes additional errors, suggesting limited generality beyond DeepSeek-style distilled models.

The confidence estimator is simplistic and weakly justified. Averaging maximum next-token probabilities over trial-answer tokens is not well calibrated as answer correctness, can be inflated by low-information formatting tokens, and is especially problematic for code where many tokens are deterministic.

Hyperparameter selection and evaluation protocol are underspecified. The paper does not clearly separate validation from test data for choosing thresholds or transition tokens, raising the risk that reported gains are tuned on the same benchmarks used for final claims.

Several benchmark results are statistically fragile. AMC 2023 and AIME 2024 have only 40 and 30 problems respectively, so large-looking percentage changes may correspond to only a few examples; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

The paper overclaims accuracy improvements despite mixed results: e.g. DEER hurts AMC 2023 for the 14B model, hurts or barely changes some programming settings, and underperforms vanilla on QwQ accuracy.

Reproducibility is limited. Important details such as exact answer-inducer prompts, transition-token sets beyond selected examples, threshold values used for each main result, accounting of failed parses, hardware/latency setup, and code availability are insufficiently specified.

The manuscript has polish issues and signs of incompleteness, including references to "Table X", forthcoming analyses, grammatical errors, and some confusing or inconsistent terminology such as "Pearl Reasoning" and "Table 7" for a figure.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, training-free and practically relevant method for reducing overthinking in reasoning models by monitoring reasoning-transition tokens, inducing trial answers, and using confidence to decide early exit.
The motivation is clear and well aligned with an important current problem: long chain-of-thought reasoning can waste compute and sometimes degrade answer quality.

The empirical results are promising across multiple benchmarks, including MATH-500, AMC 2023, AIME 2024, GPQA Diamond, HumanEval, and BigCodeBench, with substantial reported token reductions and modest-to-large accuracy gains on several settings.
The evaluation spans several DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen model sizes, showing that the method is not tied to a single parameter scale.

The paper includes useful analyses of threshold sensitivity, transition-token choice, fine-grained win/loss categories, programming tasks, and QwQ-32B transfer, which helps make the core phenomenon more credible.
The method is easy to understand and potentially easy to integrate into existing decoding pipelines, making the practical significance stronger than the algorithmic complexity might suggest.
weaknesses: The main comparison is mostly against vanilla CoT; the paper needs stronger baselines such as fixed budget forcing, concise prompting, adaptive compute methods, self-verification/probe-based early exit, and recent CoT compression or early-answer methods under matched compute budgets.

End-to-end efficiency is not fully established. The paper proposes branch-parallel decoding, but admits that more latency analysis with inference frameworks such as vLLM will appear in a future version; this is a notable gap for a paper whose central contribution is efficiency.

It is unclear whether generation length and latency accounting include all trial-answer inductions and confidence-evaluation overhead. If auxiliary branches are excluded from token accounting, the reported savings may overstate practical gains.

The threshold lambda appears empirical, and the paper does not clearly specify a principled validation protocol or whether thresholds are tuned per model/task. This raises concerns about robustness and fair test-set use.

Several reported accuracy gains are on small benchmarks such as AMC 2023 and AIME 2024, where changes of a few examples can look large; statistical uncertainty or repeated sampling analysis is missing.

Generality is only partially demonstrated. Results are strongest on DeepSeek distilled models, while QwQ-32B transfer is weaker, suggesting dependence on model-specific formatting behavior and control tokens.

The confidence metric, based on average maximum token probability of the trial answer, is simple but under-analyzed; calibration, length effects, answer-format dependence, and cases where high confidence is wrong deserve deeper treatment.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: exact transition-token sets, prompts, lambda values for all experiments, hardware, latency measurement protocol, and implementation details for branch-parallel decoding should be provided more concretely.
The writing contains some rough edges and placeholders, including references to forthcoming results and a table placeholder in related work, which makes the submission feel not fully polished.

strengths: Timely and practical problem: reducing overthinking and inference cost in long-reasoning LLMs is important, and the proposed method is simple, training-free, and plausibly easy to integrate when token logprobs and reasoning traces are available.

The paper provides a clear core idea: monitor reasoning transition points, induce a trial answer, and use the model's own token confidence to decide whether to terminate reasoning. DEER-Pro is a reasonable robustness extension via multiple prompts and MAD calibration.

Empirical coverage is broad, with experiments across many reasoning models, model sizes, and task families including math, science QA, and code generation. The reported token reductions are substantial and often accompanied by small accuracy gains.

The authors compare against several relevant efficient-reasoning baselines and include useful ablations on transition monitors, confidence aggregation, threshold sensitivity, decoding settings, and model scale.
The paper includes implementation details, prompts, pseudocode, resource information, and additional confidence interval results, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than high. The method is a clever composition of early stopping, self-confidence/logprob thresholding, and answer probing, and the paper acknowledges closely related concurrent work on trial-answer-based stopping and certainty probing.

The central evaluation metric emphasizes generated token length, but DEER incurs extra computation for trial answer induction and confidence evaluation. The latency analysis is limited to selected settings and does not fully establish production efficiency under vLLM batching, parallel serving, long induced answers, or closed-model constraints.

Accuracy gains are often small, and confidence intervals overlap in several cases. The strongest evidence is for compression, while the claim that DEER consistently improves accuracy is less firmly supported.

The method depends on access to token probabilities, reasoning delimiters/traces, and model-specific transition markers such as 'Wait'. This limits applicability to many API-only or hidden-reasoning models and may require model-specific engineering despite the paper's plug-and-play framing.

The fixed threshold lambda=0.95 is empirically reasonable but still heuristic. The paper would be stronger with calibration across domains, failure-mode analysis for overconfident wrong trial answers, and a clearer procedure for selecting thresholds without benchmark feedback.

Some baselines may not be fully comparable: TCC is set to DEER's generated length, SEAL is missing for many conditions, and Dynasor/NoThinking/CoD may not represent the strongest possible inference-time compute allocation or verifier-based baselines.

The DEER-Pro theoretical analysis relies on simplified Gaussian/i.i.d. noise assumptions for prompt-induced confidence variation; these assumptions are unlikely to hold for LLM generations, so the proof should be treated as intuition rather than strong justification.

Presentation has minor clarity and polish issues, including inconsistent naming such as DEER-Pro/DEER-PRo, occasional grammatical errors, and broad claims such as 'consistently effective' or 'eliminates prompt sensitivity' that overstate the evidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing excessive reasoning length in LRMs while preserving or improving answer accuracy.
weaknesses: The core idea is incremental: inducing intermediate answers and using model confidence/log probabilities for early stopping is closely related to existing and concurrent work on certainty probing, self-verification, adaptive stopping, and efficient CoT decoding. The paper does not convincingly establish a distinct conceptual advance.

The evaluation overstates the results. Several settings show negligible gains, overlapping confidence intervals, or accuracy drops, yet the paper repeatedly claims consistent improvement. Averaging across heterogeneous benchmarks also masks regressions on individual tasks.

The reported compression metrics appear to emphasize final output length and do not clearly account for all trial-answer generation overhead. This makes the token-reduction claims less comparable to vanilla CoT and to baselines, even though latency experiments partially address cost.

The main mechanism is confounded: improvements may come from forcing an end-of-thinking delimiter, avoiding max-length failures, answer reformatting, or exploiting benchmark answer formats rather than from reliable detection of 'pearl reasoning'. Stronger ablations are needed, such as same-token-budget sampling, forced exits at matched positions, judge/inducer-only controls, and comparisons using total generated tokens.

The method relies on access to token probabilities and model internals, limiting applicability to closed LRMs despite the broad framing around reasoning models generally. The paper should be much clearer about this deployment constraint.

The DEER-Pro theoretical analysis is weak and not very convincing. It assumes iid Gaussian prompt noise and an ill-defined 'true confidence', then derives strong robustness claims that are not well tied to actual LLM probability behavior.

The empirical study is broad but shallow in key places: small datasets such as AIME/AMC are central to the claims, yet significance and run-to-run variability are only partially addressed; prompt sensitivity, threshold tuning, and benchmark contamination risks are insufficiently analyzed.

Baselines are not fully satisfying. The strongest comparison should be against simple self-consistency/early-stop/sampling methods under equal total compute and equal token budgets, because DEER effectively performs extra generations at candidate points.

The writing and presentation are often sloppy, with grammar issues, awkward terminology such as 'pearl reasoning', overconfident language, and figures/tables that are hard to parse. This reduces confidence in the rigor of the work.

The ethics and reproducibility statements are generic. Exact code, prompts, parsing rules, outputs, and evaluation scripts are not provided in the manuscript in enough detail to make the results independently verifiable.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple, training-free dynamic early-exit mechanism for reasoning models that is well motivated by the observed overthinking phenomenon and by the pilot evidence that many examples have earlier correct stopping points.

The method is practically appealing: it uses reasoning transition points and model confidence in induced trial answers, so it can be integrated into existing open-source reasoning LLM inference pipelines without retraining.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall, covering math, science, and coding benchmarks, multiple model families and sizes, and both main-table and appendix results. The reported token reductions are substantial while accuracy is generally maintained or improved.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses: threshold sensitivity, linguistic-marker versus entropy-based transition detection, DEER versus DEER-Pro, latency measurements, early-exit rates, and confidence behavior.
The work is timely and significant for test-time scaling, where reducing unnecessary reasoning tokens without sacrificing accuracy is an important deployment problem.
weaknesses: The novelty is solid but not clearly breakthrough: the core idea is close to concurrent and related work on certainty probing, trial-answer early stopping, and adaptive inference-time compute, so the paper would benefit from sharper positioning of what is fundamentally new.

Some of the accuracy gains are modest and confidence intervals sometimes overlap, so the strongest claim is more clearly efficiency improvement with preserved accuracy than consistent accuracy improvement.

The efficiency story relies heavily on token count, while the method adds trial-answer generation and confidence computation. The latency evaluation is helpful but narrower than the benchmark evaluation and would be stronger with more details across vLLM/server settings, hardware, batch sizes, and code tasks.

The approach depends on access to token probabilities and on model-specific reasoning markers such as “Wait” or stable transition entropy. This limits applicability to closed API models and may be brittle for models/languages/reasoning styles that do not expose or follow these patterns.

Baseline tuning and fairness are not fully convincing in all cases. For example, setting TCC budgets based on DEER’s actual token length may not reflect the strongest possible budgeted prompting baseline, and some recent trained/steering approaches are discussed but not always compared directly.

Reproducibility is only partially established in the manuscript text: the abstract footnote says code is available but the visible link is missing, and several implementation details for branch-parallel decoding and evaluation extraction would need to be released to make the results easy to verify.
